skyline.text: How a miserable student nearly cost the world Oppenheimer
Ajay Shah traces one unethical culture from Roy Cohn onward
The great physicist who misjudged the scale of the Manhattan Project

brief.head: Art in the multiplex
brief.text: Christopher Nolan, Amit Varma said, brings the sensibility of the artistic filmmaker to the big screen, and studios trust him to try new things. {005-C01}

brief.head: America the backwater
brief.text: In the early 20th century, Ajay Shah said, America was a backwater. The Jewish exodus from Europe, and the move of its great intellectuals, made it take off. {005-C02}

brief.head: A frail bridge
brief.text: Oppenheimer could both understand modern physics and explain it, Ajay Shah said, a rare and important gift. “Human language is always a frail bridge of metaphors.” {005-C03}

brief.head: Technician or thinker
brief.text: Ajay Shah separates technicians, who know one narrow thing, from intellectuals, who think about the world on a larger scale. Oppenheimer, he said, was not a narrow technician. {005-C09}

brief.head: Memory runs short
brief.text: Descendants on both sides of the Oppenheimer affair still carry its memory, Ajay Shah said. In India, people of influence often lack it: “We’re very ahistorical today.” {005-C12}

thought.text: When a culture favors dull people, then that society ends up expressing those genes.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that culture, not raw talent, decides who rises to power

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s hero, and what his fall says about states
lead.head: Needed in war, hunted in peace
body: Christopher Nolan’s *Oppenheimer* was still days from release when Amit Varma and Ajay Shah recorded this episode. Shah admitted to nerves: the film’s subject had been part of his life since childhood.
“Oppenheimer died when I was one year old, and that will come as a surprise to most people, but it is not ancient history,” Shah said. “I am a visitor from the 20th century.” {005-S01}
His father passed on many stories. As a boy, Shah read Robert Jungk’s *Brighter Than a Thousand Suns* several times; as a PhD student, he found Richard Rhodes’s *The Making of the Atomic Bomb*.
## Right man, right time
Oppenheimer studied at Göttingen, then the great centre of science and mathematics, in a golden age of physics.
When Leo Szilard saw how a bomb could work and Albert Einstein wrote to President Roosevelt, the Manhattan Project began, with Oppenheimer, 38, at its head.
“Oppenheimer was the right person at the right place at the right time,” Shah said: experimentalist, theorist and gifted engineer at once.

Shah insisted that the rest of the man was no sideshow. Oppenheimer learnt Sanskrit, backed the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War and moved in communist circles. That breadth and bohemian life, Shah argued, was the source of his energy. {005-C04}
## After the bomb
“And then, of course, no good deed goes unpunished,” Shah said. Once the bomb had been exploded, traditional power structures began to assert themselves.
Oppenheimer told Truman he felt he had blood on his hands over Hiroshima and Nagasaki, which, Shah believes, made Truman very uncomfortable. {005-S06} Then he questioned the need for a hydrogen bomb.

He had angered bureaucrats by out-arguing them, and under McCarthyism he became the most famous target. A rigged process aired his private life; he was thrown out of public policy and went off to Princeton.
The story has a coda. About two years ago, Shah said, after citizens dug through the archives, the US government admitted its mistake and restored his security clearance.
## Darts and dull people

Varma took a lesson from Oppenheimer’s miserable student years, before Göttingen, when he left a poisoned apple on his physics tutor’s table. Education, Varma argued, is one-size-fits-all, and genius needs the right place.
“I think that the tragedy of Oppenheimer is not the Oppenheimer who was, but the many, many countless Oppenheimers who never even were,” he said.

Shah widened the point: the world is organised around dull people, and uses mavericks only in special moments. As Varma put it, “in extraordinary times you have to look past the mediocrity of the system because you need extraordinary people.” {005-C06}
Then, Varma said, the mediocrity of the system takes over.
“We have seven billion people in this world, and each of them is a dart,” Shah said. What shapes the world is the institutions and the culture that do the sorting. {005-C10}
The hosts closed with books. Shah’s was Rhodes’s history of the bomb, which, he said, everybody should read. Varma’s was Robert Caro’s *The Power Broker*, a study, he said, of how power corrupts.
Varma’s talk on his own hero, after whom his on-screen co-host Freddy is named, moved to the next episode: the conversation about Oppenheimer had been too delightful to cut short.

second.label: Rule of law
second.head: The state owns up
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how citizens made the US government admit its mistake
body: In the last ten years, Ajay Shah said, a group of people dug into the archives, using freedom-of-information access in the United States, and showed how the legal process against J. Robert Oppenheimer had been rigged. {005-S07}

About two years ago, the government owned up. It admitted its mistake and reinstated his security clearance. “Okay, the man is long gone, but this is very important,” Shah said. “States are cruel, coercive creatures and make mistakes all the time.”
This, for Shah, is what makes a country first-world: independent people can challenge the government and get it to retract. Indians, he said, never expect their state to admit a mistake. {005-C11}

quote.text: Being a first-world country means being a country where independent people are able to write letters and challenge the United States government.

second.caption: a state admitting its mistake

third.head: Restraint can wait
body: When Amit Varma joined Wisden in 2001, Tim de Lisle was his editor’s editor; de Lisle later edited the *Wisden Almanac*.
His tips were mostly about clarity, and Varma still uses some of his examples in the online writing course he teaches. But one tenet stood out: when in doubt, play your shots.

Varma admits he was a terrible writer then, flamboyant and always showing off, and the result was “rubbish writing”. Playing your shots, he said, also teaches you what not to do. “Restraint is something you arrive at naturally and organically over the years as you mature as an artist.” {005-S09}
He applies the rule to Christopher Nolan, whose *Interstellar* and *Tenet* move him less. He would “rather have someone trying too hard than not trying at all”. {#tryhard}
third.caption: playing your shots

p2.deck: From Göttingen to Princeton: the hero Ajay Shah grew up with, and the lessons the hosts drew

sections.label: Before the film
sections.head: An auteur, but at scale
sections.caption: Nolan, the auteur at scale
body: Amit Varma had not seen *Oppenheimer*: the episode was recorded on the Thursday before its release. But he is a big fan of Christopher Nolan, and it blows his mind that Nolan works within mainstream Hollywood.

For this film, Varma said, Nolan left Warner Brothers for Universal, because Warner now releases its films on the big screen and HBO Max simultaneously. Nolan is a stickler for the big-screen experience.

People tend to assume that intimate, artistic films go to OTT and spectacles to the theatres. Nolan straddles both worlds, and has built enough credibility to try new things rather than follow a template. “So I call him an auteur at scale, as it were,” Varma said. {005-C01}
Denis Villeneuve, he said, does the same.
## Arrival, and a restless friend
Varma’s first Villeneuve film was *Arrival*, which he saw in Bangalore with their friend Madhu Menon. Fifteen minutes in, Menon complained: “This is so slow. What is happening?” Varma was loving it.
Villeneuve’s *Blade Runner 2049* was, to Varma, better than the original, which is saying a lot: Ridley Scott’s *Blade Runner* is a masterpiece, and Scott was one of Nolan’s inspirations. {005-R12}

Ajay Shah was “trepidated”. Oppenheimer’s story is hard to tell without caricature, he said, though he felt *Dunkirk*, which Varma called one of the greatest war films he had seen, told its story well. {005-J07}
~ Despite “a Marvel cinematic universe and other such garbage”, Varma insists this is a golden age of world cinema. {005-J06}

quote.text: He brings a sensibility of the artistic filmmaker, the intimate drama, but he also cares about that cinematic experience.

sections.label: The rise
sections.head: He lit up the room
sections.caption: the making of his hero
body: Ajay Shah told the life briskly. Oppenheimer grew up in America, did some experimental physics in Britain and then went to “that great temple of the physics and the mathematics of the early 20th century”, the University of Göttingen. He got his PhD there, Shah thought, in 1927. {#phd}
Back home, at Caltech and UC Berkeley, he was legendary for being sound on the deep ideas of modern physics and for being able to explain them.
At 38 he was made head of the Manhattan Project. Whenever he walked into a room, Shah said, he lit up the room, and the conversation was always better with him in it.
## Hip, not square
About a hundred years ago, he took the trouble to learn Sanskrit. Shah offered Indians an analogy: “I’d challenge people in India to go learn Aramaic. Okay? We don’t do that.” {005-J03}

He supported the Republicans in the Spanish Civil War. His brother was in the Communist Party, and he had a lover deep inside it. In the language of the 60s, Shah said, Oppenheimer was firmly hip. {005-S05}
~ General Groves, Amit Varma added, chose him because he was good at everything except sports. “Kinda like you,” Varma told Shah. {005-J01}

quote.text: In the language of the 60s, the line between hip and square, Oppenheimer was firmly hip.

sections.label: The fall
sections.head: Blood on his hands
sections.caption: McCarthyism’s most famous target
body: Once the bomb had been exploded, Ajay Shah said, traditional power structures began to assert themselves. Oppenheimer told Truman he felt he had blood on his hands for Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and Shah believes that made Truman very uncomfortable. {005-S06}

Edward Teller pushed for a hydrogen bomb out of scientific curiosity. Oppenheimer asked what was gained by going from 20 kilotons of TNT, enough to destroy an entire city, to 200 and 2,000. {#kilotons}
He had the curse, Shah said, of knowing more than anybody else in the room, and had offended the “gray, bloodless, powerful people” on the losing side.

McCarthyism made him its most famous target. Personal information, some of it dug out illegally, was made public. Shah called it character assassination: “In today’s language, we would call it information warfare.”
## Cohn’s long shadow
The chief counsel for Joe McCarthy who tried to subpoena Oppenheimer, in 1954 “or was it 56”, Shah wondered, was Roy Cohn, later Donald Trump’s mentor. {005-S08}

Shah sees one nationalist, power-hungry, unethical culture running from McCarthy and Cohn to Trump, with people like Oppenheimer on the other side. To say there are very fine people on both sides, he said, is “not a fair statement”. {005-J13}
~ Many of today’s actors on both sides, Shah noted, are that generation’s children and grandchildren.

quote.text: Now Roy Cohn is the evil genius, the mentor, the teacher, the philosopher, the guide of Donald J. Trump.

sections.label: The lesson
sections.head: The geniuses who never were
sections.caption: mavericks and mediocrity
body: Amit Varma took a different lesson from Oppenheimer’s student years. Before Göttingen he was miserable; had he not made that lucky move, Varma said, he might have been completely wasted.

Buy potato chips and you get 40 flavours, because markets cater to different needs. {#chips} Education, designed in the 19th century to churn out workers for the industrial revolution, is one-size-fits-all.
Citing Karthik Muralidharan, he said India’s system is “optimized for sorting, not teaching”: it sorts out already-bright minds for the IITs and IIMs, and passes for good education. {005-C07}
## Mavericks on loan
Ajay Shah widened the point. Most power is controlled by people who are straight and narrow, he said, and the maverick is held at a distance. Only in special moments can the world use such people.

His example was Ukraine, where crazy people built an Uber for artillery because the country is fighting for survival. {005-J14} Oppenheimer, likewise, recruited the clever, not the obedient. When the war ended, the state no longer needed him.

Varma lamented academia’s ever-narrower silos, which end with someone “specializing in something like wheat production in Ukraine between the years 1836 to 1838”. {005-J02} Shah blamed journal and funding incentives.
~ Varma pointed to Jahnavi Phalkey’s *Atomic State*, about three scientists in 1940s India: once the extraordinary times were over, normal politics took over.

quote.text: You’re forced into silos. And those silos get narrower and narrower as time goes by.

sections.label: Amit’s pick
sections.head: A broker and his city
sections.caption: a biography of a man and a city
body: Amit Varma’s pick was Robert Caro’s *The Power Broker*, a biography of Robert Moses, a bureaucrat who gathered so much power that even the governor of New York was under his sway. {005-R03}
Varma reads it as three biographies: of a man, of New York City, and of how power corrupts.

Moses’s imagination of the city was top-down: he would build a flyover or a bridge regardless of the neighbourhood. His great opponent was Jane Jacobs, one of Varma’s intellectual heroes, who argued that cities are about people, not buildings. {005-R05}
Varma half-remembered a Winston Churchill line; Shah supplied it: “We shape our buildings and our buildings shape us.” {005-J12}

In the 1920s and 30s, Varma said, Moses seemed a brilliant, idealistic visionary. {005-C14} The book shows how power went to his ego and his politics. “It is not just about power, it’s about all of us.”
## India’s middle road

Ajay Shah said the Indian middle class yearns for an authoritarian government to tell it where the park and the metro go. India needs an urban philosophy that neither romanticises informality nor copies Chandigarh. {005-C15}
~ “I was born in Chandigarh,” Varma replied. They settled on Brasilia instead.

quote.text: An incredible study of how power corrupts, how power corrupts and corrodes the soul.

side.boxText: Even readers who think they know little science should read Richard Rhodes’s *The Making of the Atomic Bomb*, Ajay Shah said, because all great acts of creation are human projects. He found it as a PhD student and calls it the best. {005-R01}

contQuote.text: And that was the energy, the creativity, the imagination, the intellectual charisma that managed to bring all that together. You cannot separate out these parts.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: An apple, a road, a factory and a very long book

stories.caption: Oppenheimer’s poisoned apple
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Oppenheimer’s miserable student years
stories.head: An apple for the teacher, poisoned
body: Before Göttingen, J. Robert Oppenheimer was, by all accounts, a bad student. So Amit Varma told it, as he turned from Ajay Shah’s hero to the hero’s early troubles.
His physics tutor berated him for not doing enough experimental work. Oppenheimer was thinking about big ideas; he was expected to get down and dirty in the lab.

A friend who came to his room, always a chaotic mess, remembered what Oppenheimer told him: “I am having a pretty bad time. The lab work is a terrible bore, and it is impossible to feel that I am learning anything.” {#bore}
He was so unhappy that he left a poisoned apple on his tutor’s table. For a long time, Varma said, people thought the story apocryphal. But Oppenheimer admitted to it.
The university held an inquiry. His parents were wealthy, and they made sure he was not expelled, on the condition that he undergo some psychiatric treatment.

Then he went to Göttingen, “a golden place where everything fit”, Varma said. He studied under Max Born, who, Varma said, coined the term quantum physics, and had classmates like Dirac and John von Neumann. Suddenly, he flourished.
Varma set his story beside a supermarket, where potato chips come in 40 flavours. If Oppenheimer had wanted chips or shaving cream, he would have got whatever he wanted.
~ Had he not made that lucky move, Varma said, he might have been wasted. An absolute genius was almost lost, because the world did not cater to his needs. {005-S02}
stories.why: Genius depends on finding the right environment, Varma argued. An education system built on one size for all, he said, wastes the many minds that do not fit its mould.
stories.postscript: At Göttingen, Varma added, Oppenheimer was accused of being too arrogant and too confident in himself.

stories.end: atoms of uranium and turn it into either explosive energy or controlled energy
stories.caption: Szilard’s road crossing
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the idea that made the bomb buildable
stories.head: The aha moment mid-road
body: Amit Varma quoted Ernest Rutherford saying that anyone who expects a source of power from atoms “is talking moonshine”, and an early Albert Einstein saying nuclear energy would never be obtainable. {005-J09} Ajay Shah’s reply: “You gotta look at the dates of those things.”
For a long time, Shah said, E = mc² looked like a curiosity. There was not the slightest idea of the engineering. Over the next 20 or 30 years, the pieces came together.
Then Leo Szilard, crossing a road in London, had his aha moment: neutrons could trigger a chain reaction. For the first time, all the pieces clicked. {005-S03}
~ Fearing Hitler would get the bomb first, Szilard got through to Einstein, whose letter persuaded President Roosevelt to start the Manhattan Project. {005-R23}
stories.why: Scepticism, Shah argued, should be judged by when it was voiced. An idea can stay a curiosity for decades until one missing piece makes it buildable, and then, suddenly, it is an engineering project.

stories.end: and led by Oppenheimer, actually took this through to the finish line
stories.caption: Bohr’s factory
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the sheer scale of the Manhattan Project
stories.head: Turn America into a factory? Done
body: Niels Bohr had not been told about the Manhattan Project for a while, Ajay Shah said. When it was unfolded to him, he said it could not be done: “You’ll have to turn the entire United States into a factory.” Later he conceded: “and you guys did.” {005-S04}
The world’s biggest factory ever built was built for uranium enrichment, Shah said, and an even bigger facility for processing plutonium. These were challenges on a titanic scale.
A team of a couple of thousand people, inspired and led by Oppenheimer, took it through to the finish line.
~ Elsewhere Shah put the organisation Oppenheimer built at “3,000 or 6,000 interesting people”, recruited for being clever, not obedient. {#thousands}
stories.why: Even Niels Bohr misjudged what inspired leadership and organisation could achieve. Shah warned against seeing the result as inevitable: it took a particular leader, at a particular moment, to bring all the pieces together.

stories.caption: Caro’s million words
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a biography that outgrew its binding
stories.head: A million words, minus Jacobs
body: In the 1960s, Amit Varma said, Robert Caro went to a publisher with a biography of Robert Moses that he said would take a few months. It took him, Varma thinks, twelve or thirteen years, and ran to almost a million words.
The publisher insisted on one volume, because of the limits of binding, so it was cut to 800,000. Out went a book-length section that dealt mainly with Jane Jacobs.
Those 200,000 words, Varma said, are a book on Jacobs by one of the greatest biographers who ever lived. {#jacobs} They have never been made available; today an author could put them on the internet.
~ Caro then turned to Lyndon Johnson, a project still going on, with one volume left. {005-S10} His thoroughness reminded Varma of Borges’ map as big as the world. {005-R25}

quote.text: He actually took longer to write about Lyndon Johnson’s years in the Senate than Lyndon Johnson spent in the Senate.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah asked whether Caro still had his early drafts. Varma was not sure.

quiz.q: What did Niels Bohr say the Manhattan Project would require, and what did he later concede?
quiz.a: Turning the entire United States into a factory; later he said, “and you guys did.”

quiz.q: Why, according to Amit Varma, is the real tragedy not the Oppenheimer who was?
quiz.a: Because of the countless Oppenheimers who never were, lost to one-size-fits-all education.

quiz.q: Which lines from the Gita did Oppenheimer recall at the first bomb test, in Ajay Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: The Vishwarup lines: “I am become death, destroyer of the world.”

quiz.q: Who was Joe McCarthy’s chief counsel, and whom did he later mentor?
quiz.a: Roy Cohn, who became the mentor and guide of Donald J. Trump.

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma say India’s education system is optimised for, citing Karthik Muralidharan?
quiz.a: Sorting, not teaching: it picks out the already-bright and passes for good.

quiz.q: Which phrase of Jane Jacobs did Ajay Shah think about during the COVID lockdown?
quiz.a: “The ballet of the streets”, disrupted by lockdown even though the buildings remained.
